Compze/Tessaging/Typermedia/_docs/declar.title: Declaring a typermedia API | Compze
Compze/Tessaging/Typermedia/_docs/declar.summary: Declaring a typermedia API A typermedia API is made of resources: the .NET types its tueries answer with and its tommands return. A resource carries its data, and also what a caller can do next: the tueries that get related resources, its links, and the tommands that act on it, its forms. A caller never assembles a request from an identifier and a URL template: it takes the link or the form from the resource it holds, and the compiler checks that it exists. Links and forms An account resource, the link that gets it, and the tommands that act on accounts: public class AccountLink(Guid accountId) : Remotable.NonTransactional.Tueries.Tuery<AccountResource> { public Guid AccountId { get; private set; } = accountId; } public class AccountResource(Guid accountId, string email) { public Guid AccountId { get; private set; } = accountId; public string Email { get; private set; } = email; //A form the account hands out already filled in with its own id: the caller supplies only the new email. public ChangeEmail ChangeEmail(string newEmail) => new(AccountId, newEmail); } public class OpenAccount(string email) : Remotable.AtMostOnce.AtMostOnceTypermediaTommand<AccountResource> { public string Email { get; private set; } = email; } public class ChangeEmail(Guid accountId, string newEmail) : Remotable.AtMostOnce.AtMostOnceTypermediaTommand<AccountResource> { public Guid AccountId { get; private set; } = accountId; public string NewEmail { get; private set; } = newEmail; } AccountResource.ChangeEmail is a form handed out already filled in with what the resource knows, the account's id: the caller supplies only what is its to supply. A tommand that declares a result, as both of these do, answers its caller with it; one that declares none returns nothing. A resource crosses between endpoints serialized, so its state is properties the serializer can set, as in the tessages above. Its links and forms can be methods, which create them from that state. The kinds of typermedia tessage A typermedia tessage is executed: its caller waits for the handler to run and gets its result. Each kind is declared by inheriting a base class, from Compze.Tessaging.TessageTypes: Kind Declared by inheriting Executed Remotable tuery Remotable.NonTransactional.Tueries.Tuery<TResult> By the endpoint that serves it, for code in other endpoints. At-most-once typermedia tommand Remotable.AtMostOnce.AtMostOnceTypermediaTommand, or ...AtMostOnceTypermediaTommand<TResult> By the endpoint that serves it, for code in other endpoints. Strictly-local tuery StrictlyLocal.Tueries.StrictlyLocalTuery<TTuery, TResult> In its own process: see Typermedia in one process. Strictly-local tommand StrictlyLocal.Tommands.StrictlyLocalTommand, or ...StrictlyLocalTommand<TResult> In its own process. The TessageBus's exactly-once tommand is not among them: it is sent, and its sender doesn't wait for it to be handled, see Tessage types. The start Every API has a front door, the resource a caller starts from. A NewableResultLink<TResult> is a tuery that creates its result itself, with the result type's parameterless constructor, so getting the start takes no round trip: //The API's front door. Getting it takes no round trip: the caller creates the start resource itself. public static class AccountsApi { public static Remotable.NonTransactional.Tueries.NewableResultLink<AccountsStart> Start => new(); } public class AccountsStart { //A link: the tuery that gets an account. public AccountLink Account(Guid accountId) => new(accountId); //A form: the tommand that opens an account. public OpenAccount OpenAccount(string email) => new(email); } The start's links and forms lead to everything else the API offers, so a caller that knows AccountsApi.Start can reach all of it. Serving the API An endpoint serves an API by handling its tueries and tommands, each kind in an override of its declaration: class AccountsApiEndpoint : BestEffortEndpointDeclaration<AccountsApiEndpoint>, IEndpointIdentity { public static string Name => "AccountsApi"; public static EndpointId Id { get; } = new(Guid.Parse("2F6B9E1D-7C43-4A85-B0D2-93E1C8A54F07")); protected override void RegisterComponents(IComponentRegistrar registrar) => registrar .RequireMappedTypesFromAssemblyContaining<AccountLink>() .Register(Singleton.For<Accounts>().CreatedBy(() => new Accounts())); protected override void RegisterTueryHandlers(ITueryHandlerRegistrar handle) => handle .ForTuery((AccountLink link, Accounts accounts) => accounts.Get(link.AccountId)); protected override void RegisterTypermediaTommandHandlers(ITypermediaTommandHandlerRegistrar handle) => handle .ForTommand((OpenAccount tommand, Accounts accounts) => accounts.Open(tommand.Email)) .ForTommand((ChangeEmail tommand, Accounts accounts) => accounts.ChangeEmail(tommand.AccountId, tommand.NewEmail)); } A tuery handler gets a scope, and no transaction: a tuery changes nothing. A tommand handler runs in a unit of work of its own: its transactional effects commit when it returns, and roll back if it throws. Dependencies are parameters, resolved from the handler's scope: up to two for a tuery handler and one for a tommand handler. A handler that needs more takes the scope itself, an IScopeResolver or an IUnitOfWorkResolver, and resolves them from it. Exactly one handler for each type. Declaring a second one fails when it is declared. Across endpoints, when two connected endpoints serve the same type, navigating to it waits for that to resolve, and fails, naming both, when it doesn't within the navigating endpoint's patience. Best-effort and exactly-once endpoints serve typermedia alike. A tuery or tommand crosses between endpoints like any tessage, so the API's tueries and tommands are mapped to type identities, and both the serving endpoint and the endpoints that navigate it require those mappings: see type identities. The resources need no mapping. Navigating a typermedia API shows how other endpoints use it.

Compze/Tessaging/Typermedia/_docs/in-one.title: Typermedia in one process | Compze
Compze/Tessaging/Typermedia/_docs/in-one.summary: Typermedia in one process An API needn't cross processes. Strictly-local tueries and tommands are executed in the process that declares their handlers, synchronously, on the caller's thread: nothing is serialized and no endpoint is needed. The LocalTessagingEngine of Tessaging in one process executes them. Strictly-local tueries and tommands An application's account settings, as a resource with two forms: public class AccountSettingsLink : StrictlyLocal.Tueries.StrictlyLocalTuery<AccountSettingsLink, AccountSettings>; public class AccountSettings(string displayName, bool receivesNewsletter) { public string DisplayName { get; } = displayName; public bool ReceivesNewsletter { get; } = receivesNewsletter; public ChangeDisplayName ChangeDisplayName(string displayName) => new(displayName); public ToggleNewsletter ToggleNewsletter() => new(); } //Returns nothing. public class ChangeDisplayName(string displayName) : StrictlyLocal.Tommands.StrictlyLocalTommand { public string DisplayName { get; } = displayName; } //Returns the settings as they are after the change. public class ToggleNewsletter : StrictlyLocal.Tommands.StrictlyLocalTommand<AccountSettings>; A strictly-local tuery names its own type as its first type argument. Strictly-local tueries and tommands never leave their process: the remote navigator doesn't take them. So they need no type identities, and their resources need not be serializable. Declaring the handlers Typermedia handlers are declared in the engine's composition block, under a verb of their own beside RegisterTessageBusHandlers: IContainerBuilder containerBuilder = new MicrosoftContainerBuilder(); containerBuilder.Registrar .Register(Singleton.For<SettingsStore>().CreatedBy(() => new SettingsStore())) .LocalTessagingEngine(engine => engine .RegisterTypermediaHandlers(handle => handle .ForTuery((AccountSettingsLink _, SettingsStore store) => store.Current) .ForTommand((ChangeDisplayName tommand, SettingsStore store) => store.ChangeDisplayName(tommand.DisplayName)) .ForTommand((ToggleNewsletter _, SettingsStore store) => store.ToggleNewsletter()))); await using var container = containerBuilder.Build(); A tuery handler takes up to four more parameters and a tommand handler one, resolved from the scope that executes it. In an endpoint, the same handlers are declared in its declaration's RegisterTueryHandlers and RegisterTypermediaTommandHandlers overrides. Executing them Two navigators execute them, as two publishers publish tevents. Which one depends on whether the code runs inside a unit of work. Outside any unit of work, such as in an application's own classes, execute through IIndependentLocalTypermediaNavigator. It is a singleton: a class takes it as an ordinary constructor dependency. It executes each tommand as a unit of work of its own, committed when the call returns, and each tuery in a scope of its own, with no transaction: var navigator = container.RootResolver.Resolve<IIndependentLocalTypermediaNavigator>(); var settings = navigator.Execute(new AccountSettingsLink()); navigator.Execute(settings.ChangeDisplayName("Ada")); settings = navigator.Execute(settings.ToggleNewsletter()); It refuses to execute within an ambient transaction, where its execution would join that transaction instead of standing on its own. Inside a unit of work, such as in a handler, execute through ILocalTypermediaNavigatorSession, resolved from the unit of work. A tommand executes within the caller's transaction, and commits or rolls back with it; executing one with no transaction fails. A tuery executes in the caller's scope, so what it reads is consistent with what the caller has written: container.ScopeFactory.ExecuteUnitOfWork(unitOfWork => { var session = unitOfWork.Resolve<ILocalTypermediaNavigatorSession>(); var settings = session.Execute(new AccountSettingsLink()); session.Execute(settings.ChangeDisplayName("Ada Lovelace")); //Commits, or rolls back, with the unit of work. }); A handler's exception reaches the caller as it was thrown, and the handler isn't run again. Local or remote is the type's A tuery or tommand is either strictly local or remotable, and each navigator takes only its own kind: the compiler refuses a remotable tuery on a local navigator, and a strictly-local one on the remote navigator. So moving an API out of its process changes its types, not only where it is deployed, and navigation specifications, which navigate remote navigators only, have no in-process counterpart.

Compze/Tessaging/Typermedia/_docs/introd.title: Typermedia APIs | Compze
Compze/Tessaging/Typermedia/_docs/introd.summary: Typermedia APIs The most popular API in the world is a hypermedia API. You're using it right now - it's called the World Wide Web. Can you imagine trying to use it without links and forms? Instead being given an int or a string? Why do we build APIs like that? Compze extends hypermedia into Typermedia which: Routes tueries and tommands by their .NET types, giving: Zero configuration routing A simple, already well-known programming model Can be fully explored, browsed much like a website, by: Getting links: tueries Posting forms: tommands All with full type safety and autocomplete in your IDE Further encapsulates your domain, exposing less implementation details than traditional APIs All domain logic, validation, and available actions can be encapsulated in the .NET types returned by the API The UI need only bind these types to UI components without implementing any domain logic Application behavior can be fully tested without any UI framework Changing the UI becomes far less burdensome and does not risk changing domain logic Note Typermedia doesn't require distribution. An API whose tueries and tommands are strictly local is executed in its own process, synchronously, on the caller's thread: see Typermedia in one process. Distribution and asynchronous communication are optional, not a requirement. Note In-process, the performance overhead is negligible in the great majority of systems: dispatching essentially comes down to a lookup in a dictionary, with the tessage's type as the key. A first taste An account, as an accounts API returns it, carries its data and a form for changing it: public class AccountLink(Guid accountId) : Remotable.NonTransactional.Tueries.Tuery<AccountResource> { public Guid AccountId { get; private set; } = accountId; } public class AccountResource(Guid accountId, string email) { public Guid AccountId { get; private set; } = accountId; public string Email { get; private set; } = email; //A form the account hands out already filled in with its own id: the caller supplies only the new email. public ChangeEmail ChangeEmail(string newEmail) => new(AccountId, newEmail); } A client navigates from the API's start, opening an account and then changing its email, each step taking its tommand from the resource the step before returned: var openAndChangeEmail = NavigationSpecification.Get(AccountsApi.Start) .Post(start => start.OpenAccount("grace@example.com")) .Post(account => account.ChangeEmail("grace.hopper@example.com")); var grace = await navigator.NavigateAsync(openAndChangeEmail); A developer could write all of that without ever leaving their IDE. Autocomplete in the IDE makes the API browsable, not just at runtime, but as part of writing code. The same goes for all of the functionality of a domain exposed through a Typermedia API, not just the simple example above. Once you've used APIs like this, how would you feel about an API that gives you an int instead of an AccountLink? The pages, in reading order Typermedia is one of the two communication styles of Tessaging, and these pages build on Tessaging's: tueries and tommands are tessages, and remote APIs are served and navigated by endpoints. Declaring a typermedia API: resources, their links and forms, the start, and the endpoint that serves them. Navigating a typermedia API: the remote navigator, navigation specifications, and what a navigation guarantees. Typermedia in one process: strictly-local tueries and tommands, and the navigators that execute them. Typermedia is part of the Compze.Tessaging package; its tessage types are in Compze.Tessaging.Abstractions.

Compze/Tessaging/Typermedia/_docs/naviga.title: Navigating a typermedia API | Compze
Compze/Tessaging/Typermedia/_docs/naviga.summary: Navigating a typermedia API Code navigates the APIs that other endpoints serve through IRemoteTypermediaNavigator. It gets remotable tueries' results and posts at-most-once typermedia tommands, each to the one endpoint that serves its type, found the way endpoints find each other: no addresses, no routes, nothing to configure. The navigating endpoint The navigator belongs to an endpoint. This one serves nothing itself: it navigates the accounts API of Declaring a typermedia API, and requires the type mappings of its tueries and tommands: //Serves nothing: it navigates the API the AccountsApi endpoint serves. class AccountsAdminEndpoint : BestEffortEndpointDeclaration<AccountsAdminEndpoint>, IEndpointIdentity { public static string Name => "AccountsAdmin"; public static EndpointId Id { get; } = new(Guid.Parse("8C1E5A72-3D94-4F0B-A6E8-17B2D9C4E3F5")); protected override void RegisterComponents(IComponentRegistrar registrar) => registrar .RequireMappedTypesFromAssemblyContaining<AccountLink>(); } Both endpoints are hosted here in one process, in the environment of the Endpoints page. In separate processes, the code is the same: see Processes on one machine. using var registry = InterprocessEndpointRegistry.OpenOrCreateSessionLocal("AccountsApiExample.EndpointRegistry", dataDirectory); await using var host = EndpointHost.Production.Create(() => new MicrosoftContainerBuilder(), new SameMachineEnvironment(registry, dataDirectory)); host.RegisterEndpoint(new AccountsApiEndpoint()); var admin = host.RegisterEndpoint(new AccountsAdminEndpoint()); await host.StartAsync(); var navigator = admin.ServiceLocator.Resolve<IRemoteTypermediaNavigator>(); The navigator is a singleton, so an application's own classes take it as an ordinary constructor dependency. One step at a time GetAsync gets a tuery's result, PostAsync posts a tommand and returns its result, and each has a synchronous form, Get and Post: var start = await navigator.GetAsync(AccountsApi.Start); var ada = await navigator.PostAsync(start.OpenAccount("ada@example.com")); ada = await navigator.PostAsync(ada.ChangeEmail("ada.lovelace@example.com")); Each step takes its tuery or tommand from the resource the step before returned. Getting the start takes no round trip: it creates its result itself. Navigation specifications A NavigationSpecification describes a whole navigation as one value, step by step, and runs nothing until it is navigated: var openAndChangeEmail = NavigationSpecification.Get(AccountsApi.Start) .Post(start => start.OpenAccount("grace@example.com")) .Post(account => account.ChangeEmail("grace.hopper@example.com")); var grace = await navigator.NavigateAsync(openAndChangeEmail); NavigationSpecification.Get(tuery) starts at a tuery, and tommand.Post() at a tommand. Get follows a link, and Post submits a form, each built from the result of the step before. Select takes what the navigation is after from the result of the step before, with no round trip: var gracesEmail = NavigationSpecification.Get(AccountsApi.Start) .Get(start => start.Account(grace.AccountId)) .Select(account => account.Email) .NavigateOn(navigator); A specification navigates on any remote navigator, with navigator.NavigateAsync(specification), navigator.Navigate(specification) or specification.NavigateOn(navigator), and can be navigated as often as needed. So an API can publish its common navigations as specifications, for its clients to navigate as they are or to extend with more steps. A specification whose last step posts a tommand that returns nothing navigates only synchronously, with NavigateOn. What a navigation guarantees It waits for a server. A navigation to a type that no connected endpoint serves waits for one, within the navigating endpoint's handler-availability patience, and a navigation to a type that two connected endpoints serve waits for that to resolve: see Readiness and waiting sends. Never within a transaction. Navigating from code within a transaction fails at once: a remote tuery or tommand can't take part in the caller's transaction, so it never seems to. Only other endpoints. An endpoint's navigator reaches the APIs that other endpoints serve. A type that only the navigating endpoint serves is never found: navigating to it waits, then fails as if nothing served it. A handler's failure reaches the caller. When a handler throws, the navigation fails with TessageDispatchingFailedException, whose message holds the handler's exception, as text: its type doesn't cross. A tommand's transactional effects commit at most once for each post. A tommand handler that throws is run again at once, in a new unit of work, up to five times in all. Its effects outside the transaction happen again with each try, such as an email sent. A tuery handler that throws is not run again. Nothing deduplicates posts. Posting the same tommand twice executes it twice. The navigator never posts again by itself, so when a post fails on its way, the caller can't tell whether the tommand was executed.

Compze/Tessaging/_docs/delivery-guarante.title: Delivery guarantees | Compze
Compze/Tessaging/_docs/delivery-guarante.summary: Delivery guarantees A tessage's type declares what its delivery guarantees, and the endpoints honor it: neither the code that publishes or sends it nor the code that handles it chooses. An endpoint that can't honor what a type declares refuses it, loudly, when it is declared or when it is published: a guarantee is never silently weakened. The four ways a tevent reaches a handler Each way gives up one thing the one above it has: What it is Gives up Participation Handlers in the publishing endpoint run within the publisher's transaction, before the publish returns. A failing handler fails the publish. Exactly-once The tevent is stored in the publisher's transaction, and each subscribing endpoint handles it exactly once, in a transaction of its own. Taking part in the publisher's transaction. Best-effort The tevent is sent to the subscribing endpoints, which handle it in a transaction of their own. Nothing is stored, deduplicated or retried. The certainty that it arrives. Observation Observers watch committed tevents, outside every transaction. Transactions. Which way a tevent reaches a handler is decided like this: Every handler in the publishing endpoint participates, whatever the tevent's type. A handler in another endpoint receives it exactly once or best-effort, as the tevent's type declares: IExactlyOnceTevent exactly once, any other IRemotableTevent best-effort. An ITevent that is not remotable never leaves the endpoint that publishes it. An observer observes, wherever it is. Every way delivers a remote tevent on commit: a tevent whose publisher's transaction rolls back reaches no other endpoint. Exactly-once delivery An exactly-once tevent or tommand is written to the sending endpoint's outbox within the sender's transaction, so it is sent if, and only if, the sender's change commits. The outbox delivers it until the receiving endpoint has stored it in its inbox, through network failures and restarts on either side. The receiving endpoint deduplicates it by its Id, and handles it in a transaction that also records that it was handled, so its handler's transactional effects commit once. A subscriber that is down gets it when it returns. An exactly-once tevent goes to every endpoint whose subscription the publisher remembers, not only to those connected when it is published. An endpoint remembers every other endpoint it has met, with what that endpoint handles and subscribes to. A tommand is bound to one receiver when it is sent: the endpoint that handles its type and is connected, or else the one remembered endpoint that handles it. When that endpoint is down, the tommand waits for it. In order. What one endpoint sends another, tevents and tommands alike, the other receives in the order the sending transactions committed, across restarts on either side. An endpoint handles its exactly-once tessages one at a time, in the order they arrived. A failing handler is retried, a few times. When a handler throws, its transaction rolls back and it is run again at once, up to five times in all. After the fifth failure the tessage is recorded as failed, and isn't handled again; the endpoint goes on with the next. Best-effort delivery A best-effort tevent is sent to each endpoint that subscribes to it. Its handlers there run in a transaction of their own, so their effects are atomic, but nothing is stored, deduplicated or retried, and a handler that throws is logged and not run again. Best-effort is still the best effort the publisher can make: it doesn't drop tevents merely because a subscriber is away. Held while a subscriber is down. The publisher keeps, in memory, a queue for each endpoint it remembers as a subscriber. Tevents published while that endpoint is down wait in the queue, and are delivered, in order, when it returns. In order. A subscriber receives the tevents in the order they were published. What can be lost: what was published before a subscriber was first met, the one tevent being delivered when a delivery fails, and what is queued when the publisher's process ends. A failed delivery pauses the queue until the subscriber answers again: the tevents behind the lost one are delivered, in order, never skipped. Bounded. A queue holds at most 10,000 tevents. A publish that would overflow one fails with BestEffortTeventQueueOverflowException, naming the subscriber. Two declarations adjust this for chosen endpoints: RequiredPeers: endpoints this one requires. Everything published before a required endpoint is first met is held for it, so tevents aren't lost to the moments it takes the endpoints to find each other at startup. PeersNotQueuedFor: endpoints this one keeps nothing for. A tevent reaches such an endpoint only while it is connected. Consistency: the endpoint is the boundary After each unit of work an endpoint is consistent, not eventually consistent: what one tessage's handling changed in the endpoint has been changed in full, by the handlers of every tevent it published there, within the same transaction. Where a handler lives decides when it runs: Within the endpoint, at once. A tevent's handlers in the publishing endpoint participate in the publish, and a tommand whose handler is in the sending endpoint is handled at once, within the sender's unit of work: no outbox, no inbox, and exactly once because it is one transaction. In another endpoint, eventually, with the guarantee its type declares. So moving a handler to another endpoint is a decision about consistency, and it is visible where it is made, in the declarations. The price of the boundary is that everything within it runs in one transaction: each participating handler adds to the time it holds its locks. When that costs too much, split the endpoint, observe instead of participating, or send a tommand to an endpoint that does the work later. What isn't there yet Forgetting an endpoint. An endpoint remembers every endpoint it has met, and nothing yet makes it forget one. What is owed an endpoint that never returns waits for it: exactly-once tessages in the outbox, and best-effort tevents in memory until the queue's bound fails the publishes. Administering failed tessages. A tessage whose handling failed five times stays recorded as failed in the inbox, and nothing yet shows or retries it.

Compze/Tessaging/_docs/endpoints.html.title: Endpoints | Compze
Compze/Tessaging/_docs/endpoints.html.summary: Endpoints An endpoint is what lets tessages cross between parts of a system that don't share a container. It is the engine of one process given an identity and a wire: a container of its own, the handlers its declaration declares, and a transport server through which the other endpoints reach it. One process may host one endpoint or several. Endpoints in the same process converse through their transport, exactly as endpoints in different processes do, so moving an endpoint to a process of its own changes nothing about how it converses. Two kinds of endpoint Best-effort endpoint Exactly-once endpoint Declared by inheriting BestEffortEndpointDeclaration<TIdentity> ExactlyOnceEndpointDeclaration<TIdentity> Needs a database No. Yes: it joins a domain database. Tevents it publishes Local ones (ITevent) and best-effort ones (IRemotableTevent). Every kind, exactly-once ones (IExactlyOnceTevent) included. Tevents it receives Best-effort ones. Best-effort ones and exactly-once ones. Tommands it sends and handles None of the TessageBus's. Exactly-once tommands. What it remembers about other endpoints For as long as its process runs. In its database, across restarts. Both serve tueries and typermedia tommands. An exactly-once endpoint keeps an inbox and an outbox in its domain database: they are what make its deliveries exactly-once. A best-effort endpoint asked to publish an exactly-once tevent refuses: a guarantee is never silently weakened. Declaring an endpoint An endpoint is declared as a class. These declare two endpoints that converse with each other through these tessages: public class RegisterAccount(Guid accountId, string email) : Remotable.ExactlyOnce.Tommand { public Guid AccountId { get; private set; } = accountId; public string Email { get; private set; } = email; } public interface IAccountRegistered : IExactlyOnceTevent { Guid AccountId { get; } string Email { get; } } public class AccountRegistered(Guid accountId, string email) : IAccountRegistered { public TessageId Id { get; private set; } = new(); public Guid AccountId { get; private set; } = accountId; public string Email { get; private set; } = email; } public class RecordWelcomeEmailSent(Guid accountId) : Remotable.ExactlyOnce.Tommand { public Guid AccountId { get; private set; } = accountId; } The Accounts endpoint registers accounts, and records that their welcome emails were sent: class AccountsEndpoint : ExactlyOnceEndpointDeclaration<AccountsEndpoint>, IEndpointIdentity { public static string Name => "Accounts"; public static EndpointId Id { get; } = new(Guid.Parse("0E4C7B3A-5D21-4F8E-9A6B-2C1D8E7F3A95")); protected override void RegisterComponents(IComponentRegistrar registrar) => registrar .RequireMappedTypesFromAssemblyContaining<RegisterAccount>() .Register(Singleton.For<AccountRecords>().CreatedBy(() => new AccountRecords())); protected override void RegisterExactlyOnceTommandHandlers(IExactlyOnceTommandHandlerRegistrar handle) => handle .ForTommand((RegisterAccount tommand, IUnitOfWorkTeventPublisher publisher) => publisher.PublishAsync(new AccountRegistered(tommand.AccountId, tommand.Email))) .ForTommand((RecordWelcomeEmailSent tommand, AccountRecords records) => records.RecordWelcomeEmailSentAsync(tommand.AccountId)); } The WelcomeEmails endpoint sends a welcome email for each registered account, and tells the Accounts endpoint that it did: class WelcomeEmailsEndpoint : ExactlyOnceEndpointDeclaration<WelcomeEmailsEndpoint>, IEndpointIdentity { public static string Name => "WelcomeEmails"; public static EndpointId Id { get; } = new(Guid.Parse("7A2F9C14-8B3E-4D6A-B105-E94C2D6F8B37")); protected override void RegisterComponents(IComponentRegistrar registrar) => registrar .RequireMappedTypesFromAssemblyContaining<RegisterAccount>() .Register(Singleton.For<IEmailSender>().CreatedBy(() => new ConsoleEmailSender())); protected override void RegisterExactlyOnceTeventHandlers(IExactlyOnceTeventHandlerRegistrar handle) => handle .ForTevent(async (IAccountRegistered registered, IEmailSender emailSender, IUnitOfWorkTommandSender tommandSender) => { await emailSender.SendWelcomeEmailAsync(registered.Email); await tommandSender.SendAsync(new RecordWelcomeEmailSent(registered.AccountId)); }); } Identity A declaration usually is its own identity: it implements IEndpointIdentity, whose static Name and Id it builds under. The Name is for humans. The EndpointId is the endpoint's identity across processes and restarts, so it is a fixed Guid, written once and never changed. Code that refers to another endpoint refers to its identity type, such as AccountsEndpoint.Id, and the compiler checks the reference. When several processes must refer to an endpoint that only one of them declares, its identity can be a type of its own, in an assembly they share: see Processes on one machine. An exactly-once endpoint's name prefixes its tables in the domain database, so it is a letter followed by letters, digits and underscores, at most 28 characters long. What a declaration overrides A declaration overrides only what its endpoint uses. Each kind of handler has its override, which gets a registrar that can register only that kind, so a handler of the wrong kind can't be registered: Override Registers Endpoint RegisterExactlyOnceTommandHandlers handlers of exactly-once tommands exactly-once RegisterExactlyOnceTeventHandlers handlers of exactly-once tevents exactly-once RegisterBestEffortTeventHandlers handlers of the other tevents both ObserveTevents observers both RegisterTueryHandlers, RegisterTypermediaTommandHandlers Typermedia's handlers both RegisterComponents the endpoint's other components, and the type identities it needs both RequiredPeers, PeersNotQueuedFor, HandlerAvailabilityPatience how it treats other endpoints: see Delivery guarantees and Readiness and waiting sends both Declare anything else, on the endpoint's whole builder, such as a tevent store both A best-effort endpoint's declaration has no overrides for exactly-once handlers: it has no database to deliver them exactly once with. A subscription in the wrong override fails when the endpoint is built, naming the override it belongs in. Note An exactly-once handler's effects within its transaction happen exactly once. A side effect outside the transaction, such as the email above, happens again if the handler fails after it and is retried. Type identities A tessage that crosses between endpoints carries the identity of its type, and that identity must survive renaming and moving the type. So every type that crosses is mapped to a Guid, in a class its assembly declares: using Compze.TypeIdentifiers; using Compze.Tessaging.Documentation.DeclaringEndpoints; using Compze.Tessaging.Documentation.OnOneMachine; using Compze.Tessaging.Typermedia.Documentation.DeclaringAnApi; [assembly: AssemblyTypeMapper(typeof(Compze.Tessaging.Documentation.TessageTypeMappings))] namespace Compze.Tessaging.Documentation; class TessageTypeMappings : IAssemblyTypeMapper { public void Map(IAssemblyTypeMappingRegistrar map) => map .Map<RegisterAccount>("632b961b-1b64-4747-bb5e-a76a9b46b58f") .Map<IAccountRegistered>("cb849aa3-e951-4334-9118-9dd55003378c") .Map<AccountRegistered>("eefb3f2d-256f-4a00-a280-07a62239959d") .Map<RecordWelcomeEmailSent>("d95c7d8d-bc07-41f1-91cd-bccb24704497") .Map<IIndexingProgressed>("599d64e1-18e7-4384-90be-d70609045d4d") .Map<IndexingProgressed>("1579d6ff-cc6d-4112-891f-51240ea20bba") .Map<AccountLink>("bd50a225-57bf-47bc-9908-62a28e270103") .Map<OpenAccount>("7b462fba-4035-4d12-b3d9-80954eaa7417") .Map<ChangeEmail>("b4d311a4-1214-4e33-a81c-3d36043d0980"); } Map the tommands sent, the tevent interfaces subscribed to, and the tevent classes published. Each endpoint then declares, in RegisterComponents, the assemblies whose types it needs, with RequireMappedTypesFromAssemblyContaining<T>(): those of the types it sends, publishes, handles and subscribes to, and those of every type that the endpoints it converses with handle or subscribe to. An endpoint that handles or subscribes to a type it can't map fails when it is built, naming the type. Warning An endpoint connects to another only if it can map every type the other handles and subscribes to. When it can't, it logs a warning at each attempt to connect, and its sends to that endpoint wait, then fail as if nothing handled their tessages. The environment What a declaration doesn't say is where its endpoint runs: the transport, the serializer, how it finds the other endpoints, and, for an exactly-once endpoint, the domain database it joins. An IEndpointEnvironment says that, once for every endpoint of a deployment: class SameMachineEnvironment : IEndpointEnvironment { readonly InterprocessEndpointRegistry _registry; readonly DirectoryInfo _dataDirectory; public SameMachineEnvironment(InterprocessEndpointRegistry registry, DirectoryInfo dataDirectory) { _registry = registry; _dataDirectory = dataDirectory; } public void Configure(EndpointBuilder endpointBuilder) => endpointBuilder .NamedPipeEndpointTransport() .NewtonsoftSerializer() .ParticipateIn(_registry); public void ConfigureDomainDatabase(ExactlyOnceEndpointBuilder endpointBuilder) { endpointBuilder.Registrar.Register(Singleton.For<IConfigurationParameterProvider>() .CreatedBy(() => new SqliteFilesIn(_dataDirectory))); endpointBuilder.SqliteDomainDatabase("Accounts"); } } //Gives every connection string name a sqlite database file of its own in the data directory. class SqliteFilesIn(DirectoryInfo dataDirectory) : IConfigurationParameterProvider { readonly DirectoryInfo _dataDirectory = dataDirectory; public string GetString(string parameterName, string? valueIfMissing = null) => $"Data Source={Path.Combine(_dataDirectory.FullName, parameterName + ".sqlite")}"; } Note In an ASP.NET Core project, whose implicit usings include Microsoft.AspNetCore.Builder, the name EndpointBuilder is ambiguous. using EndpointBuilder = Compze.Tessaging.Endpoints.EndpointBuilder; resolves it. The same declaration builds in any environment, so production and tests host the same endpoint, in different environments. The domain database is the domain's, not the endpoint's: any number of exactly-once endpoints join one, each with tables of its own, and the database holds the domain's own data too, so that an endpoint's handlers change the domain and record their tessages in one transaction. The domain database is reached through connection strings, by name, from the container's IConfigurationParameterProvider. On SQLite, an endpoint whose domain database is named Accounts uses three databases: Accounts, Accounts.PeerRegistry and Accounts.TypeIdInterner. The environment above gives each a file of its own in a data directory. Hosting An EndpointHost builds each registered declaration in its environment, on a new container builder from the factory it was given, and starts and disposes them together: using var registry = InterprocessEndpointRegistry.OpenOrCreateSessionLocal("AccountsExample.EndpointRegistry", dataDirectory); await using var host = EndpointHost.Production.Create(() => new MicrosoftContainerBuilder(), new SameMachineEnvironment(registry, dataDirectory)); var accounts = host.RegisterEndpoint(new AccountsEndpoint()); host.RegisterEndpoint(new WelcomeEmailsEndpoint()); await host.StartAsync(); var tommandSender = accounts.ServiceLocator.Resolve<IIndependentTommandSender>(); await tommandSender.SendAsync(new RegisterAccount(Guid.NewGuid(), "ada@example.com")); The sent RegisterAccount is handled at once, within the send's own unit of work, since its handler is in the sending endpoint; the AccountRegistered that its handler publishes crosses to the WelcomeEmails endpoint, and the RecordWelcomeEmailSent that WelcomeEmails sends crosses back. Delivery guarantees explains why the first stays and the others cross. Application code outside any handler reaches an endpoint's components through its ServiceLocator, as the sending code above does. The host is a convenience: an endpoint's declaration can build it without one, with Build(containerBuilder, environment), and the endpoint starts and stops itself. The lifecycle Starting runs three phases in order: the endpoint listens on a new address, announces the address, and starts sending. An announced address is therefore always one that is listening. When StartAsync completes the endpoint has started; finding the other endpoints goes on from there, and readiness awaits it. Stopping runs the phases in reverse: it retracts the address, stops sending and stops listening, then lets what was already received finish. Disposing an endpoint stops it first. A stopped endpoint never starts again. One process at a time. An exactly-once endpoint runs in one process at a time: starting it in a second process fails with EndpointAlreadyRunningInAnotherProcessException. The lock that ensures it dies with its process, so after a crash the endpoint can start again at once.

Compze/Tessaging/_docs/in-one-process.ht.title: Tessaging in one process: the LocalTessagingEngine | Compze
Compze/Tessaging/_docs/in-one-process.ht.summary: Tessaging in one process: the LocalTessagingEngine Many applications need Tessaging only inside one process: tevents that decouple the parts of an application from each other, published by one part and handled by the others. For that, a container composes the LocalTessagingEngine, and nothing else: there is no endpoint, no transport and no host, and everything but observation runs on the caller's thread. Composing the engine The engine is composed into a container in one block, which declares every handler it will ever have: using Compze.DependencyInjection; using Compze.DependencyInjection.Abstractions; using Compze.DependencyInjection.Microsoft; using Compze.Tessaging.Engine; using Compze.Tessaging.Engine.Wiring; using Compze.Tessaging.TessageBus; using Compze.Tessaging.Documentation.DeclaringTessageTypes; IContainerBuilder containerBuilder = new MicrosoftContainerBuilder(); containerBuilder.Registrar .Register(Singleton.For<AccountStatistics>().CreatedBy(() => new AccountStatistics()), Singleton.For<AccountRegistration>().CreatedBy((IIndependentTeventPublisher publisher) => new AccountRegistration(publisher))) .LocalTessagingEngine(engine => engine .RegisterTessageBusHandlers(handle => handle .ForTevent((IAccountRegistered registered) => Console.WriteLine($"Welcome, {registered.Email}!")) .ForTevent((IAccountTevent tevent, AccountStatistics statistics) => statistics.Record(tevent)))); await using var container = containerBuilder.Build(); One engine per container. Composing a second one fails. The declaration is the only way in. The engine's handlers are fixed when the container is built: nothing can register a handler later. Handlers take what they need. A handler takes the tevent, and up to two more parameters, which are resolved from the scope of the unit of work that delivers the tevent. A handler can be synchronous, or return a Task. The same declaration block is what an endpoint's handlers are declared through, so these handlers run unchanged when the application later becomes several endpoints. Publishing tevents Two interfaces publish tevents. Which one depends on whether the code runs inside a unit of work: a scope of the container paired with a System.Transactions transaction, begun together and completed together, so that all its effects commit or roll back as one. Outside any unit of work, such as in an application's own classes, publish through IIndependentTeventPublisher. It is a singleton, so a class takes it as an ordinary constructor dependency, and each publish runs as a unit of work of its own: class AccountRegistration { readonly IIndependentTeventPublisher _publisher; public AccountRegistration(IIndependentTeventPublisher publisher) => _publisher = publisher; public Guid Register(string email) { var accountId = Guid.NewGuid(); _publisher.Publish(new AccountRegistered(accountId, email)); return accountId; } } var registration = container.RootResolver.Resolve<AccountRegistration>(); var accountId = registration.Register("ada@example.com"); //Prints "Welcome, ada@example.com!" before it returns. It refuses to publish within an ambient transaction, since its publish would join that transaction instead of standing on its own. Inside a unit of work, such as in a handler, publish through IUnitOfWorkTeventPublisher. A handler takes it as one of its parameters; code that begins a unit of work itself resolves it from the unit of work: container.ScopeFactory.ExecuteUnitOfWork(unitOfWork => { var publisher = unitOfWork.Resolve<IUnitOfWorkTeventPublisher>(); publisher.Publish(new AccountEmailChanged(accountId, "ada.lovelace@example.com")); publisher.Publish(new AccountImported(Guid.NewGuid(), "grace@example.com", importedFrom: "the old system")); }); It refuses to publish without an ambient transaction, since there is no unit of work to publish within. Both have a Publish and a PublishAsync. PublishAsync publishes every kind of tevent; Publish refuses an IExactlyOnceTevent, whose publishing writes to a database within the transaction. What publishing does In the publishing process, a published tevent's handlers participate in the publish: They run before Publish returns, on the publisher's thread, within the publisher's transaction. They run in the order they were declared, whichever types they subscribe to, so a handler may rely on what the handlers declared before it did. A handler that throws fails the publish. The exception reaches the publisher, and the unit of work rolls back, with the effects of the handlers that ran before it. A handler may publish tevents in turn, through the IUnitOfWorkTeventPublisher it takes as a parameter; their handlers participate in the same unit of work. That makes a handler part of the publisher's change: the publisher and its handlers commit together or not at all. A reaction that should happen only once the change has committed, and should never fail it, is an observer instead. Stopping Stop the engine before disposing the container: await container.RootResolver.Resolve<ILocalTessagingEngine>().StopAsync(); Stopping waits, holding no thread, for the observers to observe every tevent committed so far, and then refuses new publishes. Disposing a container that wasn't stopped stops the engine first. What a container without endpoints doesn't have A tevent published in a container with no endpoint reaches the handlers in that container, and only them. Sending an exactly-once tommand takes an exactly-once endpoint: IUnitOfWorkTommandSender and IIndependentTommandSender are registered by those endpoints, not by the engine. The engine also executes strictly-local tueries and tommands, through ILocalTypermediaNavigatorSession and IIndependentLocalTypermediaNavigator: see Typermedia.

Compze/Tessaging/_docs/introduction.html.title: Tessaging | Compze
Compze/Tessaging/_docs/introduction.html.summary: Tessaging Tessaging is Compze's messaging. Code that has something done, or that tells the rest of the system what happened, sends a message, and the handlers that should receive it do, without the sender and the handlers knowing about each other. What sets Tessaging apart is that a message's .NET type is its whole contract: Compze calls such a type-routed message a tessage. No routing configuration. There are no topic names, queue names or routing keys. A tessage goes to the handlers of its type, and a subscriber to IAccountTevent receives every tevent whose type implements IAccountTevent, including kinds of tevent added long after the subscriber was written. The type declares the guarantees. Whether a tessage may leave its process, and whether its delivery is best-effort or exactly-once, is declared by the interfaces its type implements: neither the sender nor the receiver configures it. One model, from one process to many. The same handler declarations run in a single process's container and in endpoints that converse across processes. Moving a handler to another process is a change of deployment, and the guarantees its tessages declare move with it. Note Compze's packages are pre-release: their APIs still change from one version to the next. The tessage kinds Kind It says Who handles it tevent Something happened. Every handler subscribed to a compatible type: none, one or many. tommand Do this. Exactly one handler. tuery Answer this. Exactly one handler, which changes nothing. Two ways to converse Tessaging carries two communication styles: TessageBus: tell, and trust that it arrives. Code publishes tevents and sends tommands, and doesn't wait for the handlers in other endpoints to run. These pages cover the TessageBus, and what the two styles share. Typermedia: ask, and get the answer now. Tueries and typermedia tommands are executed like requests to a browsable API: see Typermedia. A first taste A container composes the LocalTessagingEngine with a handler for each tevent type it cares about: IContainerBuilder containerBuilder = new MicrosoftContainerBuilder(); containerBuilder.Registrar .Register(Singleton.For<AccountStatistics>().CreatedBy(() => new AccountStatistics()), Singleton.For<AccountRegistration>().CreatedBy((IIndependentTeventPublisher publisher) => new AccountRegistration(publisher))) .LocalTessagingEngine(engine => engine .RegisterTessageBusHandlers(handle => handle .ForTevent((IAccountRegistered registered) => Console.WriteLine($"Welcome, {registered.Email}!")) .ForTevent((IAccountTevent tevent, AccountStatistics statistics) => statistics.Record(tevent)))); await using var container = containerBuilder.Build(); Publishing a tevent runs every handler whose type it is compatible with: var registration = container.RootResolver.Resolve<AccountRegistration>(); var accountId = registration.Register("ada@example.com"); //Prints "Welcome, ada@example.com!" before it returns. The pages, in reading order Tessage types: declaring tevents, tommands and tueries, and what their types promise. In one process: the LocalTessagingEngine, handlers, and publishing tevents. Observing tevents: watching what has happened, outside every transaction. Endpoints: declaring, configuring and hosting the endpoints that converse with each other. Delivery guarantees: what each guarantee means, ordering, and the consistency of an endpoint. Processes on one machine: several processes forming one application, with no configuration. Readiness and waiting sends: startup and restarts without races. The packages Package What it brings Compze.Tessaging.Abstractions The tessage types and the publishing and sending interfaces: all a contracts assembly needs. Compze.Tessaging The LocalTessagingEngine, endpoints, and the named-pipe transport. Compze.DependencyInjection.Microsoft A container to compose in. Autofac, DryIoc and LightInject have packages too. Compze.Hosting EndpointHost, and the InterprocessEndpointRegistry that endpoints on one machine discover each other through. Compze.Serialization.Newtonsoft The serializer every endpoint declares. Compze.Tessaging.Sqlite The domain database of exactly-once endpoints, on SQLite. Compze.Tessaging.MicrosoftSql, .PostgreSql and .MySql serve the database servers. Compze.TypeIdentifiers and Compze.TypeIdentifiers.DependencyInjection The stable identities of the types that cross between endpoints.

Compze/Tessaging/_docs/observing-tevents.title: Observing tevents | Compze
Compze/Tessaging/_docs/observing-tevents.summary: Observing tevents A handler takes part in the change that published its tevent: it runs within the publisher's transaction, and its failure fails the publish. Many reactions should do neither. A view that refreshes, a read model that updates, a notification: each reacts to what has happened, and the change that happened shouldn't wait for it, nor fail because of it. Such a reaction is an observer. It watches tevents that have been committed, and stands outside every transaction. What an observer can rely on Committed tevents only. A tevent is queued for its observers when the unit of work that published it commits. A tevent whose unit of work rolls back is never observed. Off the publisher's thread. Observers run on threads of their own: an observer's slowness never delays the publisher, and its failure never reaches it. In order. Each observer has a queue of its own, and observes tevents in the order they were committed. A slow observer delays only itself. Once. An observer never observes a tevent twice. No transaction. Each call gets a fresh scope of the container, with no transaction. Failures are reported, not retried. A throwing observer's exception is logged as an error, and the observer goes on with its next tevent. Observers and handlers run independently of each other, so nothing orders an observer's call relative to the handlers of an arriving tevent. Composed observers Observers that live as long as the container are declared next to the handlers, under a verb of their own: containerBuilder.Registrar.LocalTessagingEngine(engine => engine .ObserveTevents(observe => observe .ForTevent((IAccountRegistered registered) => Console.WriteLine($"Observed the registration of {registered.Email}")) .ForTeventsOfEachUnitOfWork((IReadOnlyList<IAccountTevent> tevents) => Console.WriteLine($"A unit of work changed accounts {tevents.Count} times")))); ForTeventsOfEachUnitOfWork observes the tevents of each committed unit of work as one list, in the order they were published: for a reaction that is costly for each call, such as refreshing a view or writing a read model to a database. It is never called with an empty list. A tevent with no unit of work known to its process, one published through IIndependentTeventPublisher or one that arrives from another endpoint, comes as a list of its own. Like a handler, an observer takes up to two more parameters, resolved from its scope. Dynamic observers Some observers come and go while the application runs, such as one for each open view. IDynamicTeventObservers creates them, and disposing what it returns ends them: class AccountListView : IDisposable { readonly IDisposable _observation; public AccountListView(IDynamicTeventObservers observers) => _observation = observers.ObserveTevents(observe => observe.ForTevent((IAccountTevent tevent) => Refresh(tevent))); void Refresh(IAccountTevent tevent) => Console.WriteLine($"The account list shows the change to account {tevent.AccountId}"); public void Dispose() => _observation.Dispose(); } A dynamic observer observes the tevents committed after ObserveTevents returns. Disposing it drops what is queued for it and not yet started, and doesn't wait for a call that is already running, so a view disposed on its UI thread can't deadlock with an observer that waits for that thread. Waiting for the observers A batch job or a tool that reports, exports or backs up once the observers have caught up waits for them: await engine.AwaitNoTessagesInFlightAsync(); It waits, holding no thread, until every tevent committed so far has been observed by every observer of it, including what the observers publish meanwhile. Tevents that other code publishes during the wait may or may not be waited for, so it is for code that controls what runs. Observers in an endpoint An endpoint declares composed observers by overriding ObserveTevents, and they observe the tevents that arrive from other endpoints as well as those committed in its own process. An arriving tevent was committed by its publisher, so it is queued for its observers as it arrives. An endpoint asks the other endpoints for the tevents it subscribes to when it starts. So a dynamic observer in an endpoint may observe only types the endpoint subscribed to for it, in its declaration's Declare override: class AccountViewsEndpoint : ExactlyOnceEndpointDeclaration<AccountViewsEndpoint>, IEndpointIdentity { public static string Name => "AccountViews"; public static EndpointId Id { get; } = new(Guid.Parse("190bbc33-1577-4beb-9e53-9c738635adc0")); protected override void RegisterComponents(IComponentRegistrar registrar) => registrar .RequireMappedTypesFromAssemblyContaining<RegisterAccount>(); protected override void Declare(ExactlyOnceEndpointBuilder endpoint) => endpoint .SubscribeForDynamicObservers<IAccountRegistered>(); } Observing a remote exactly-once tevent takes an exactly-once endpoint: it is received exactly once, through the endpoint's inbox, like any subscription to it.

Compze/Tessaging/_docs/on-one-machine.ht.title: Processes on one machine | Compze
Compze/Tessaging/_docs/on-one-machine.ht.summary: Processes on one machine An application may be several processes on one machine: say a desktop application, a background indexer and a tray helper, each hosting endpoints that converse with the others'. Tessaging connects them with no web server, no ports or addresses to configure, and no database server: each process declares its endpoints and names the registry the application's processes share. Named pipes, and an address for each start The named-pipe transport is part of Compze.Tessaging, built on .NET's own pipes, so a process loads no web stack for it. An endpoint declares it in its environment with NamedPipeEndpointTransport(). A new address each time an endpoint starts. Addresses are never configured, nor written down anywhere: the endpoint's EndpointId is what identifies it, and discovery finds where it listens now. Only the same user. A pipe accepts connections only from processes that run as the user that created it. Windows, Linux and macOS. On Linux and macOS, .NET's pipes are Unix domain sockets. The interprocess registry Endpoints announce their addresses to an InterprocessEndpointRegistry, and find each other's there. Its state is a memory-mapped file, so it needs no server, and what one process announces is visible at once to the others: Its name and directory make the application. The processes that open the registry of the same name, in the same directory, in the same login session, find each other's endpoints. Another application opens a registry of its own. ParticipateIn(registry) declares both sides, finding the others through it and announcing the endpoint to it. DiscoverEndpointsThrough and AnnounceAddressTo declare one side each. A crashed process's addresses disappear. Each announcement records the process that made it, and an address whose process no longer runs is never listed. An endpoint doesn't connect once and assume the result. It keeps its connections in line with what the registry lists now: an endpoint that appears is connected to, one that leaves is dropped, and one that restarts at a new address is reconnected, with what was waiting for it. An announcement wakes the other processes at once; a crash, which announces nothing, is noticed within a second. An application of two processes This application's indexer process reports its progress to its desktop process, with best-effort tevents: neither process stores anything, so neither needs a database. The tevents, and the identities of the two endpoints, are in an assembly both processes reference. An endpoint's identity is a type of its own here, rather than its declaration, because the indexer refers to the desktop's endpoint, which only the desktop process declares: //In an assembly both processes reference. public sealed class DesktopEndpoint : IEndpointIdentity { public static string Name => "Desktop"; public static EndpointId Id { get; } = new(Guid.Parse("3B8E1F42-C6D9-4A57-8E20-F1A93C5D7B64")); } public sealed class IndexerEndpoint : IEndpointIdentity { public static string Name => "Indexer"; public static EndpointId Id { get; } = new(Guid.Parse("C5A04D93-17E2-4B8F-A639-0D72E8B4F1C6")); } public interface IIndexingProgressed : IRemotableTevent { int FilesIndexed { get; } } public class IndexingProgressed(int filesIndexed) : IIndexingProgressed { public int FilesIndexed { get; private set; } = filesIndexed; } Both processes run their endpoints in the same environment: class DesktopSuiteEnvironment : IEndpointEnvironment { readonly InterprocessEndpointRegistry _registry; public DesktopSuiteEnvironment(InterprocessEndpointRegistry registry) => _registry = registry; public void Configure(EndpointBuilder endpointBuilder) => endpointBuilder .NamedPipeEndpointTransport() .NewtonsoftSerializer() .ParticipateIn(_registry); //Called only for exactly-once endpoints, and this suite has none: nothing in it is stored anywhere. public void ConfigureDomainDatabase(ExactlyOnceEndpointBuilder endpointBuilder) => throw new NotSupportedException("The desktop suite's endpoints are all best-effort endpoints."); } The desktop process handles the indexer's tevents: class DesktopEndpointDeclaration : BestEffortEndpointDeclaration<DesktopEndpoint> { protected override void RegisterComponents(IComponentRegistrar registrar) => registrar .RequireMappedTypesFromAssemblyContaining<IIndexingProgressed>(); protected override void RegisterBestEffortTeventHandlers(IBestEffortTeventHandlerRegistrar handle) => handle .ForTevent((IIndexingProgressed progressed) => Console.WriteLine($"{progressed.FilesIndexed} files indexed")); } static class DesktopProcess { internal static async Task RunAsync(DirectoryInfo suiteDirectory, Task applicationExit) { using var registry = InterprocessEndpointRegistry.OpenOrCreateSessionLocal("DesktopSuite.EndpointRegistry", suiteDirectory); await using var host = EndpointHost.Production.Create(() => new MicrosoftContainerBuilder(), new DesktopSuiteEnvironment(registry)); host.RegisterEndpoint(new DesktopEndpointDeclaration()); await host.StartAsync(); await applicationExit; } } The indexer process publishes them: class IndexerEndpointDeclaration : BestEffortEndpointDeclaration<IndexerEndpoint> { //Tevents published before the desktop is discovered are held for it, not lost. protected override IReadOnlyList<EndpointId> RequiredPeers => [DesktopEndpoint.Id]; protected override void RegisterComponents(IComponentRegistrar registrar) => registrar .RequireMappedTypesFromAssemblyContaining<IIndexingProgressed>(); } static class IndexerProcess { internal static async Task RunAsync(DirectoryInfo suiteDirectory, Task applicationExit) { using var registry = InterprocessEndpointRegistry.OpenOrCreateSessionLocal("DesktopSuite.EndpointRegistry", suiteDirectory); await using var host = EndpointHost.Production.Create(() => new MicrosoftContainerBuilder(), new DesktopSuiteEnvironment(registry)); var indexer = host.RegisterEndpoint(new IndexerEndpointDeclaration()); await host.StartAsync(); var publisher = indexer.ServiceLocator.Resolve<IIndependentTeventPublisher>(); foreach(var filesIndexed in new[] { 100, 200, 300 }) publisher.Publish(new IndexingProgressed(filesIndexed)); await applicationExit; } } The two processes start in either order. The indexer requires the desktop's endpoint, so the tevents it publishes before the two have found each other are held for the desktop, and delivered once they have. For tommands and tueries sent before their handlers are found, see Readiness and waiting sends. Exactly-once across processes Exactly-once endpoints need a domain database, and on one machine SQLite database files do with nothing to install: the environment on the Endpoints page gives each its file in a data directory. An exactly-once endpoint runs in one process at a time, so two processes that share a domain database host different endpoints of it. Across machines Compze's transports reach endpoints on the same machine today: named pipes, and HTTP through ASP.NET Core (Compze.Tessaging.Transport.AspNetCore), which listens on the loopback interface. Endpoints on different machines can't converse yet.

Compze/Tessaging/_docs/readiness-and-wai.title: Readiness and waiting sends | Compze
Compze/Tessaging/_docs/readiness-and-wai.summary: Readiness and waiting sends Endpoints find each other after they start, and an endpoint that restarts is away for a moment. A tessage sent in such a moment, to a handler not yet found or briefly gone, doesn't fail at once. What happens instead depends on its kind: A tevent is held for the endpoints that will receive it: see Delivery guarantees. An exactly-once tommand whose handler the endpoint remembers is stored in the outbox, bound to that handler's endpoint, and delivered when it is back. The send doesn't wait. A tommand or tuery whose handler can't be reached waits for it, and goes ahead the moment it can. This is a waiting send. Waiting sends A send waits when no handler of its tessage's type is reachable: a tuery or a typermedia tommand when no endpoint that handles it is connected, and an exactly-once tommand when it can't be bound to one endpoint: none that handles it has been met, or several have and none of them is connected. It waits for the endpoint's handler-availability patience, 30 seconds unless its declaration says otherwise: class SignupEndpoint : ExactlyOnceEndpointDeclaration<SignupEndpoint>, IEndpointIdentity { public static string Name => "Signup"; public static EndpointId Id { get; } = new(Guid.Parse("E81B3C57-0F4A-4D92-B6C8-5A27D9E1F043")); //A send with no reachable handler waits up to this long for one, instead of the default 30 seconds. protected override TimeSpan? HandlerAvailabilityPatience => TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10); protected override void RegisterComponents(IComponentRegistrar registrar) => registrar .RequireMappedTypesFromAssemblyContaining<RegisterAccount>(); } When the patience runs out, the send fails with NoHandlerForTessageTypeException for an exactly-once tommand, and NoHandlerForTypermediaTypeException for a tuery or typermedia tommand. The message tells the two causes apart: an endpoint that handles the type is remembered and is down, or no endpoint ever met handles it, which is most likely an endpoint not deployed or not configured to find this one. A send that could never succeed fails at once instead, such as one of a type that isn't remotable. Readiness Waiting sends make the first callers after a start pay for the endpoints finding each other. An application that would rather pay before it takes any traffic awaits its endpoint's readiness: await host.StartAsync(); //Completes once a handler is reachable for every tommand and tuery in RegisterAccount's namespace. await signup.AwaitReadinessAsync(ReadinessTypes.InNamespaceOf<RegisterAccount>()); //Only now open the doors to traffic: no first caller pays for discovery. AwaitReadinessAsync completes when the endpoint can reach a handler for each of the types: its own handlers count, an exactly-once tommand counts when its handler's endpoint is connected or remembered, and a tuery or typermedia tommand when exactly one endpoint that handles it is connected. These are the conditions under which a send doesn't wait. ReadinessTypes gathers the types by reflection, so that a type added later isn't forgotten: ReadinessTypes.InAssemblyContaining<T>(): those in T's assembly. ReadinessTypes.InNamespaceOf<T>(levelsToWalkUpBeforeRecursingDown): those in T's namespace and the namespaces below it, after walking up the given number of levels. ReadinessTypes.These(...): the types named. They take only tueries, typermedia tommands and exactly-once tommands, the kinds that have one handler to wait for, and fail at once on an empty set or a type of another kind. Readiness waits as long as the endpoint's handler-availability patience, or as long as its patience argument says, then fails with EndpointNotReadyWithinPatienceException, naming every type still unreachable, and why. Readiness is the readiness probe an orchestrator calls, and the place to give up on a misconfigured deployment once, at startup, rather than through every call that times out. It covers startup; waiting sends cover the moments of a restart, later.

Compze/Tessaging/_docs/tessage-types.htm.title: Tessage types: the type is the contract | Compze
Compze/Tessaging/_docs/tessage-types.htm.summary: Tessage types: the type is the contract Every tessage is an instance of a .NET type, and that type says everything about it: its kind, who may receive it, whether it may leave its process, and what its delivery guarantees. The interfaces it implements, all in the Compze.Tessaging.TessageTypes namespace, are how it says so. Tevents: interfaces in a hierarchy A tevent says that something happened. Declare tevents as interfaces that inherit each other, each adding the meaning that sets it apart: public interface IAccountTevent : ITevent { Guid AccountId { get; } } public interface IAccountRegistered : IAccountTevent { string Email { get; } } public interface IAccountImported : IAccountRegistered { string ImportedFrom { get; } } public interface IAccountEmailChanged : IAccountTevent { string Email { get; } } Classes implement them. Only the code that publishes a tevent knows its class: public class AccountRegistered(Guid accountId, string email) : IAccountRegistered { public Guid AccountId { get; private set; } = accountId; public string Email { get; private set; } = email; } public class AccountImported(Guid accountId, string email, string importedFrom) : IAccountImported { public Guid AccountId { get; private set; } = accountId; public string Email { get; private set; } = email; public string ImportedFrom { get; private set; } = importedFrom; } public class AccountEmailChanged(Guid accountId, string email) : IAccountEmailChanged { public Guid AccountId { get; private set; } = accountId; public string Email { get; private set; } = email; } Routing by type A tevent is delivered to every handler whose subscribed type it is compatible with: the rule is .NET's own type compatibility, so routing is polymorphism. Given these subscriptions: .ForTevent((IAccountTevent tevent) => Console.WriteLine($"Every account tevent: {tevent.GetType().Name}")) .ForTevent((IAccountRegistered registered) => Console.WriteLine($"Registrations, imports included: {registered.GetType().Name}")) .ForTevent((IAccountImported imported) => Console.WriteLine($"Imports only: {imported.GetType().Name}")) Published IAccountTevent handler IAccountRegistered handler IAccountImported handler AccountRegistered ✔ ✔ AccountImported ✔ ✔ ✔ AccountEmailChanged ✔ That is what makes a hierarchy of tevents worth designing: a subscriber says precisely what it cares about, and keeps receiving it whatever is added later. A new kind of registration, IAccountRegisteredBySupport : IAccountRegistered, reaches the IAccountRegistered subscribers with no change to them. Routing configuration, and type checks in handlers, have nothing left to do. Tip Subscribe to interfaces, never to tevent classes. A subscriber to a class misses every tevent of the classes added later, and the classes are the publisher's implementation detail to refactor as it likes. Designing a hierarchy of tevents, for an entity that publishes them, is what Teventive is about. What a tevent's type promises about its delivery Three interfaces declare how far a tevent travels and what its delivery guarantees. The publisher and the subscribers choose none of it: //Never leaves the process that publishes it. public interface IAccountCacheInvalidated : ITevent; //May cross to other endpoints, best-effort: no store, no deduplication, no retries. public interface IAccountsOnlineCountChanged : IRemotableTevent { int AccountsOnline { get; } } //Crosses to other endpoints exactly once: stored, deduplicated, its handling retried when it fails. public interface IAccountClosed : IExactlyOnceTevent { Guid AccountId { get; } } public class AccountClosed(Guid accountId) : IAccountClosed { public TessageId Id { get; private set; } = new(); //What the receiving endpoint deduplicates on. public Guid AccountId { get; private set; } = accountId; } The tevent implements It travels Its delivery ITevent Within the process that publishes it. Its handlers there run within the publisher's transaction. IRemotableTevent Also to the endpoints that subscribe to it. Best-effort: no store, no deduplication, no retries. IExactlyOnceTevent Also to the endpoints that subscribe to it. Exactly once: stored in the publisher's transaction, deduplicated by its Id, its handling retried when it fails. Delivery guarantees says what each guarantee means in full. Tommands: exactly one handler A tommand tells its one handler to do something. The tommand of the TessageBus is the exactly-once tommand: it is delivered to its handler exactly once, wherever the handler is, and the sender doesn't wait for it to be handled. The Remotable.ExactlyOnce.Tommand base class gives a tommand the Id its deduplication needs: public class CloseAccount(Guid accountId) : Remotable.ExactlyOnce.Tommand { public Guid AccountId { get; private set; } = accountId; } It is sent through IUnitOfWorkTommandSender or IIndependentTommandSender, which exactly-once endpoints provide: see Endpoints. Typermedia has tommands of its own, whose callers wait for them to be handled, and may get a result: strictly-local tommands, executed in-process, and at-most-once typermedia tommands, executed by another endpoint: see Typermedia. Tueries: a question with one answer A tuery asks its one handler for an answer, and changes nothing. Its type declares the type of its result: public class AccountDetails(Guid accountId, string email) { public Guid AccountId { get; private set; } = accountId; public string Email { get; private set; } = email; } public class AccountDetailsTuery(Guid accountId) : Remotable.NonTransactional.Tueries.Tuery<AccountDetails> { public Guid AccountId { get; private set; } = accountId; } Tueries are Typermedia's: see Typermedia. One handler, and declarations that fail loud A tommand type and a tuery type have exactly one handler each: declaring a second handler for one fails when it is declared. A tevent type has any number. The framework also refuses a type that contradicts itself, such as one that is both a tommand and a tevent, or both remotable and strictly local. It checks a type the first time the type is sent or subscribed to. To check a whole vocabulary at once, from a test, point TessageTypeDesignRules at the assemblies that declare it: TessageTypeDesignRules.AssertFulfilledByAllTessageTypesIn(typeof(IAccountTevent).Assembly); It reports every violating type in one failure.

Compze/Teventive/Taggregates/_docs/defin.title: Tevents | Compze
Compze/Teventive/Taggregates/_docs/defin.summary: Note You are absolutely not expected to understand all the how's and why's of this definition the first time you read it. Think of it as combination cheat sheet and teaser. Tevents Declare their meaning through their type Tevents use the type system of the language in which they are implemented to declare their meaning, in as much detail and as unambiguously as possible. All the semantics of the event should be part of the declaration of the event type. Are always interfaces In .Net tevents are always interfaces, because to encode meaning in detail multiple inheritance is required. Some class will implement the interface, but you always subscribe to interfaces and design in terms of interfaces. Implements ITevent Every tevent implements ITevent Are routed by type compatibility The type of a tevent is the means through which tevents are routed to subscribers. Every single type-compatible registered handler method, local or remote, will be called when a tevent is published. To illustrate: Given that the method void HandleTevent(ISomeTevent tevent) is registered as a tevent handler, then every single tevent that can be assigned to a variable of type ISomeTevent will be delivered to HandleTevent This type compatibility includes support for generic covariance Interface inheritance is not enough to model realistic domains effectively. To support inheritance of tevent based taggregates, and reusable tevent based components, tevents leverage generic covariance. The covariant wrapper interface is IPublisherTevent<out TTevent>: a wrapper whose own type identifies the tevent's publisher while its type parameter carries the wrapped tevent's full type. For example: this handler: void HandleTevent(IPublisherTevent<ITevent> tevent) would be called whenever any type of IPublisherTevent<T> was published. IPublisherTevent<IUserTevent>, IPublisherTevent<IAnimalTevent> and so on. Likewise, given a publisher-specific wrapper interface IAnimalTevent<out T> : IPublisherTevent<T>; when any IAnimalTevent<T> was published, the above handler would also be called.

Compze/Teventive/Taggregates/_docs/intro.title: Introduction to tevents | Compze
Compze/Teventive/Taggregates/_docs/intro.summary: So what does all of that mean in practice? Let's dive right in to some code illustrating tevents. This is the root of the tevent inheritance hierarchy. By some level of indirection, every tevent implements it: public interface ITevent; Every tevent published by a taggregate will implement this interface: public interface ITaggregateTevent : ITevent { Guid TaggregateId { get; } } Every tevent that means a taggregate was created will implement this interface. public interface ITaggregateCreatedTevent : ITaggregateTevent; Let's use User as an example taggregate. Here's the root of the User taggregate tevent hierarchy: interface IUserTevent : ITaggregateTevent; And of course things can happen related to users: interface IUserCreated : IUserTevent, ITaggregateCreatedTevent; interface IUserRegistered : IUserCreated; interface IUserImported : IUserRegistered; Now stop and look carefully at how the tevents so far implement each other. This is the core concept of tevents. That the relationship in meaning between tevents can be modeled using .Net type compatibility, and that we can use the same mechanism to listen to exactly the tevents we need. Most of this information is declared by implementing various interfaces. Let's examine a simple example of what this means in practice. Here's how you might subscribe to these tevents: registrar .ForTevent<IUserTevent>(userTevent => WriteLine($"User: {userTevent.TaggregateId} something happened")) .ForTevent<IUserRegistered>(userRegistered => WriteLine($"User: {userRegistered.TaggregateId} registered")) .ForTevent<IUserImported>(userImported => { WriteLine($"User: {userImported.TaggregateId} imported"); return Task.CompletedTask; }); Now let's see if your intuition is on target here. When an IUserImported tevent is published, What will be the output? The correct answer is: User: SOME-GUID something happened User: SOME-GUID registered User: SOME-GUID imported An IUserImported tevent is compatible with all the registered handlers, and will therefore be delivered to all of them in the order that the handlers were registered. If an IUserTevent was published only the first subscriber would be called, if an IUserRegistered was published, the first two would be called.

Compze/Teventive/Taggregates/_docs/prope.title: Property updated tevents | Compze
Compze/Teventive/Taggregates/_docs/prope.summary: Adding properties to our tevents You may have noticed that the tevents on the last page were missing a little something, namely properties. Now the natural expectation would be for a slightly more realistic version of something like this: interface IUserRegistered : IUserTevent, ITaggregateCreatedTevent; interface IUserChangedEmail : IUserTevent; to be something like this: interface IUserRegistered : IUserTevent, ITaggregateCreatedTevent { Email Email { get; } } interface IUserChangedEmail : IUserTevent { Email Email { get; } } However, doing that does not work well at all. The dilemma of Fine-grained vs Coarse-grained events The reason the above code is terrible idea, is that some tevent listeners care only about updated data, and others care about semantics. If we do things like above, the code that care only about data will not only have to know about and manually listen to every single concrete tevent in the system that updates Email, we must keep track of every such listener for every single taggregate property in our whole system, and update the effected ones every time a new tevent that updates any taggregate property is created 😨 Classically the above problem has lead to projects being forced to choose between using fine-grained property-updated events and coarse-grained semantically meaningful domain events. The problem is that both choices are maintainability disasters. If you go with property-updated style events you lose virtually all ability to understand the semantics of what happened, as a single user interaction is exploded into a number of individual data atoms 😬 If you go with coarse-grained events, we run head first into the issues described in the previous paragraph. You cannot win as long as you accept the choice. Unifying Fine-grained and Coarse-grained events With tevents you don't need to choose. If you do this: interface IUserEmailPropertyUpdated : IUserTevent { Email Email { get; } } interface IUserRegistered : IUserEmailPropertyUpdated, ITaggregateCreatedTevent; interface IUserChangedEmail : IUserEmailPropertyUpdated; The whole problem disappears like it never existed ☺️ When we design tevents like that, a listener like this ... registrar .ForTevent<IUserEmailPropertyUpdated>(emailUpdated => { WriteLine($"User: {emailUpdated.TaggregateId} Email: {emailUpdated.Email}"); return Task.CompletedTask; }); ... will never need to change throughout the whole lifetime of the system. It will be called whenever a user's email is updated. Period. Likewise, listeners that care about when users are registered will listen to IUserRegistered and receive the same benefits. No matter how many new ways of registering users we add, no matter how many new subtypes of IUserRegistered are added. That code will always be called and does not need to change. A better perspective?
