Rather than saying that some listeners care only about data, and not semantics, it may be better to say that they care about different aspects of semantics, of the meaning of the tevent. That IUserRegistered changes the Email property of a User is part of the semantics of the tevent and to be properly designed that means that the tevent must implement another tevent that declares this meaning. Without that, the declaration of IUserRegistered is semantically incomplete and that is why we run into trouble.

Compze/Teventive/Taggregates/_docs/reusa.title: Reusable tevent based components and entities | Compze
Compze/Teventive/Taggregates/_docs/reusa.summary: Note Taggregate specific nested components and entities are fully supported already. We've already shown examples of how tevents for them look. You just nest component/entity tevent interfaces within your root tevent interface. Simple. What we are discussing on this page is how to create tevent based components and entities that can be used in multiple different tevent based taggregates without code duplication. That is another ballgame. Reusable tevent based components and entities So as in the note above, the question is how we go about it when there is some sort of component or entity that we want to be able to reuse in multiple different taggregates without code duplication. We would consider any approach to modeling that did not support this without breaking a sweat to be badly limited. Since it is a shared, reusable component: It cannot publish taggregate tevents, that must be up to the taggregate. We must be able to subscribe to the published tevents by type, meaning that the tevent ultimately published by the taggregate must declaratively, statically, contain the type of the tevent from the component. One taggregate may hold several of the same component, so the taggregate, and its subscribers, must be able to tell them apart. Thankfully the solution to inheriting taggregates has taken us most of the way to a solution for this problem too. We will just need to wrap one more time, generic covariance to the rescue once more. Compze calls such a component a shared tomponent: a teventive component, which publishes tevents and applies them to its own state, that is tied to no particular taggregate. The taggregate that holds it, or the component of a taggregate that does, is its owner. And the owner's class declares a slot for each shared tomponent it holds. Let's build one: a price, which products and bundles of products both have. A product has two of them, a list price and a sale price. The shared tomponent's own tevents A shared tomponent's tevents are rooted in a tevent interface of its own, which implements nothing but ITevent. They carry no taggregate id and say nothing of which taggregate they happen in. Only the owner knows that. interface IPriceTevent : ITevent { interface IChanged : IPriceTevent { decimal Amount { get; } } } Something must implement the interfaces. The classes mirror them: abstract class PriceTevent : IPriceTevent { internal class Changed(decimal amount) : PriceTevent, IPriceTevent.IChanged { public decimal Amount { get; } = amount; } } The shared tomponent class Price : SharedTomponent<IPriceTevent> { static readonly TeventRouting<Price, IPriceTevent> Appliers = DeclareAppliers<Price>(it => it .For<IPriceTevent.IChanged>(static (price, changed) => price.Amount = changed.Amount)); protected override TeventRouting TeventAppliers => Appliers; public Price(SharedTomponentSlotInAnOwner<IPriceTevent> slot) : base(slot) {} public decimal Amount { get; private set; } public void ChangeTo(decimal amount) => Publish(new PriceTevent.Changed(amount)); } It derives from SharedTomponent<IPriceTevent>, typed on its own tevent root. Its state changes only in its tevent appliers, just as a taggregate's does. ChangeTo doesn't set Amount: it publishes a tevent, and the applier of that tevent sets Amount, when the tevent is published and again whenever the taggregate's history is replayed. Its appliers are declared once for the class, with DeclareAppliers, kept in a static field, and handed to the base class by overriding the protected TeventAppliers property. More on that below. Its constructor takes a SharedTomponentSlotInAnOwner<IPriceTevent>: the slot it is in, in its owner, which the owner hands it, as we'll see. That is how Publish knows where the tevent goes. It knows nothing of products, or of bundles. The owner's tevents adopt the shared tomponent's The product's tevents are those of any taggregate: a root tevent interface, and a wrapper interface for it, as on the taggregate inheritance page. We'll come to IRepriced in a moment. interface IProductTevent : ITaggregateTevent { interface ICreated : IProductTevent, ITaggregateCreatedTevent { string Name { get; } } interface IRepriced : IProductTevent; } interface IProductTevent<out T> : ITaggregateTevent<T> where T : IProductTevent; abstract class ProductTevent : TaggregateTevent, IProductTevent { protected ProductTevent() {} ProductTevent(TaggregateId taggregateId) : base(taggregateId) {} internal class Created(TaggregateId taggregateId, string name) : ProductTevent(taggregateId), IProductTevent.ICreated { public string Name { get; } = name; } } class ProductTevent<T>(T tevent) : TaggregateTevent<T>(tevent), IProductTevent<T> where T : IProductTevent; Now the new part. For each slot, the owner declares an adopting wrapper tevent: a tevent of the owner that wraps a tevent of the shared tomponent. interface IProductListPriceTevent<out T> : IProductTevent.IRepriced, IPublisherTevent<T> where T : IPriceTevent; interface IProductSalePriceTevent<out T> : IProductTevent.IRepriced, IPublisherTevent<T> where T : IPriceTevent; Read IProductListPriceTevent<out T> like this: it is a product tevent, here one that means the product was repriced, and it is an IPublisherTevent<T>, the covariant wrapper of a price tevent. So it says three things at once: what happened, which is T; which taggregate it happened in, a product; and in which member of the product, the list price. The two slots wrap the very same price tevents: only their adopting wrapper tevents tell them apart. Each adopting wrapper tevent has a class implementing it: class ProductListPriceTevent<T>(T tevent) : ProductTevent, IProductListPriceTevent<T> where T : IPriceTevent { public T Tevent { get; } = tevent; } class ProductSalePriceTevent<T>(T tevent) : ProductTevent, IProductSalePriceTevent<T> where T : IPriceTevent { public T Tevent { get; } = tevent; } When the list price changes, the product publishes an IProductTevent<IProductListPriceTevent<IPriceTevent.IChanged>>. That is the price's tevent, adopted by the list price slot, and then wrapped, as every tevent a product publishes is, in the wrapper that says which class of product published it. Two wrappings, each covariant. The slot the owner's class declares static class Slots { internal static readonly SharedTomponentSlot<Product, IProductTevent, ProductTevent, IPriceTevent, IProductListPriceTevent<IPriceTevent>> ListPrice = new(typeof(ProductListPriceTevent<>), static product => product.ListPrice); internal static readonly SharedTomponentSlot<Product, IProductTevent, ProductTevent, IPriceTevent, IProductSalePriceTevent<IPriceTevent>> SalePrice = new(typeof(ProductSalePriceTevent<>), static product => product.SalePrice); } A SharedTomponentSlot holds what is the same for every product: The class implementing the slot's adopting wrapper tevent, as an open generic type. The slot closes it over each tevent's own type, so the published tevent carries the full type of what happened. How to get the shared tomponent in this slot from a product. Its five type arguments are the owner's class, the owner's tevent root and the class implementing it, the shared tomponent's tevent root, and the adopting wrapper tevent closed over that root. The slots are static: declared once, shared by every product, and costing a product nothing. Keep them in a nested static class, such as Slots. The runtime then creates them before they are first used, wherever the routing that uses them is written. Declared beside the routing in the owner's class itself, a slot would have to be written above it, since a class's static fields are initialized in the order written. The product constructs each price with its slot in this product: Slots.ListPrice.In(this). Product() { ListPrice = new Price(Slots.ListPrice.In(this)); SalePrice = new Price(Slots.SalePrice.In(this)); } public string Name { get; private set; } = ""; public Price ListPrice { get; } public Price SalePrice { get; } An owner can also be a component of a taggregate. A slot in a component is declared, constructed with, and routed exactly as in a taggregate. Routing tevents back to the shared tomponent static readonly TeventRouting<Product, IProductTevent> Appliers = DeclareAppliers(it => it .For<IProductTevent.ICreated>(static (product, created) => product.Name = created.Name) .SharedTomponent(Slots.ListPrice) .SharedTomponent(Slots.SalePrice)); protected override TeventRouting TeventAppliers => Appliers; Every teventive class, whether a taggregate, a component or a shared tomponent, declares its tevent routing once: which tevent applier each tevent reaches. DeclareAppliers declares it, and the class keeps it in a static field and returns it from its override of the protected TeventAppliers property. Every instance of the class shares it. For<T> routes every tevent assignable to T to an applier. The applier is a static lambda that gets the instance as its first parameter: the routing is shared by every instance, so it can hold no state of its own. SharedTomponent(slot) routes every tevent in that slot's adopting wrapper tevent to the shared tomponent in that slot, which applies it through its own routing. A tevent reaches every route it matches, one after another, in the order they were declared. A class that inherits from another extends its base class's routing with Extend, and the base class's routes come first. So an applier can rely on those declared before it having applied the same tevent. A tevent that reaches no applier is an error, unless the routing lets it go with IgnoreUnhandled. So when the list price changes, var product = Product.Create("Teapot"); product.ListPrice.ChangeTo(25m); the list price slot wraps the change in a ProductListPriceTevent<>, the product publishes that as its own tevent, the product's routing routes it through the list price slot back to the list price, and the list price's applier sets its Amount. The sale price never sees it. The mistakes that are easy to make are loud: A class that doesn't override TeventAppliers doesn't compile. A subclass that inherits its base class's routing, instead of extending it, is refused when it is first constructed. A slot handed a class that doesn't implement its adopting wrapper tevent, such as another slot's, throws when the slot is made. A shared tomponent constructed with another slot than the one whose member it is kept in throws when it first publishes, and when its owner's history is loaded. Subscribing to a shared tomponent's tevents To follow the list price of every product, subscribe to the whole published tevent: registrar.ForTevent<IProductTevent<IProductListPriceTevent<IPriceTevent.IChanged>>>( changed => WriteLine($"Product {changed.Tevent.TaggregateId}: the list price is now {changed.Tevent.Tevent.Amount}")); The handler gets the published tevent as it stands: changed.Tevent is the adopting wrapper tevent, a product tevent carrying the product's id, and changed.Tevent.Tevent is the price's own tevent. The adopting wrapper tevent is a tevent of the owner, so it can say what the change means to the owner. Both price slots' adopting wrapper tevents are IProductTevent.IRepriced, so this subscriber hears of every change to either price, and of nothing else: registrar.ForTevent<IProductTevent.IRepriced>(repriced => WriteLine($"Product {repriced.TaggregateId} was repriced")); In the same way, a subscriber to IProductTevent gets every adopting wrapper tevent along with the product's other tevents. And since every adopting wrapper tevent is an IPublisherTevent<>, a subscriber can follow a shared tomponent's tevents in every slot of every owner without knowing any of them. This one hears of every price change, in products and bundles alike: registrar.ForTevent<IPublisherTevent<IPublisherTevent<IPriceTevent.IChanged>>>( changed => WriteLine($"A price is now {changed.Tevent.Tevent.Amount}")); Warning A subscription sees one level of wrapping. A subscription to a type that is no wrapper is matched against what the published wrapper wraps, and a subscription to a wrapper type is matched against the published wrapper itself. A shared tomponent's tevent is wrapped twice, so: A subscriber to IPriceTevent.IChanged receives nothing: what the product's wrapper wraps is the adopting wrapper tevent, not the change. A subscriber to IProductListPriceTevent<IPriceTevent.IChanged> receives nothing either: it is a wrapper type, and the published wrapper is the product's. Wrap it once more, and it receives the list price's changes: IPublisherTevent<IProductListPriceTevent<IPriceTevent.IChanged>>. Reusable entities: shared tentities A shared tentity is to an entity what a shared tomponent is to a component: a teventive entity, with an id of its own, written once, which any taggregate can keep a collection of. Reviews are an example. Every tevent of a review carries, as ordinary domain data, the id of the review it belongs to: its EntityId. interface IReviewTevent : ISharedTentityTevent<ReviewId> { interface IWritten : IReviewTevent { int Stars { get; } } interface IAnswered : IReviewTevent { string Answer { get; } } } abstract class ReviewTevent(ReviewId entityId) : IReviewTevent { public ReviewId EntityId { get; } = entityId; internal class Written(ReviewId entityId, int stars) : ReviewTevent(entityId), IReviewTevent.IWritten { public int Stars { get; } = stars; } internal class Answered(ReviewId entityId, string answer) : ReviewTevent(entityId), IReviewTevent.IAnswered { public string Answer { get; } = answer; } } class Review : SharedTentity<Review, ReviewId, IReviewTevent, IReviewTevent.IWritten> { static readonly TeventRouting<Review, IReviewTevent> Appliers = DeclareAppliers(it => it .For<IReviewTevent.IWritten>(static (review, written) => review.Stars = written.Stars) .For<IReviewTevent.IAnswered>(static (review, answered) => review.Answer = answered.Answer)); protected override TeventRouting TeventAppliers => Appliers; public Review(SharedTentityCollection<Review, ReviewId, IReviewTevent, IReviewTevent.IWritten> reviews) : base(reviews) {} public int Stars { get; private set; } public string? Answer { get; private set; } public void AnswerWith(string answer) => Publish(new ReviewTevent.Answered(Id, answer)); } ReviewId is a small value type of the example's own, around a Guid. A review derives from SharedTentity<Review, ReviewId, IReviewTevent, IReviewTevent.IWritten>: its own class, its id, its tevent root, and the tevent that creates one. Its routing starts with an applier of the base class's, which gives a new review the EntityId of its created tevent as its Id. The review's own applier of IWritten comes after it. A review publishes tevents that carry its own Id, and Publish asserts that they do. The owner keeps its reviews in a SharedTentityCollection, which is itself a shared tomponent: it takes one slot, and every review in it publishes through that slot's adopting wrapper tevent. The collection creates a review when a created tevent arrives, and routes every other tevent to the review whose id it carries. A review is added by publishing its created tevent, with AddByPublishing, which returns the new review. Start to finish: a second owner A bundle of products has a price too, and reviews. Here is all of it: interface IBundleTevent : ITaggregateTevent { interface ICreated : IBundleTevent, ITaggregateCreatedTevent { string Name { get; } } } interface IBundleTevent<out T> : ITaggregateTevent<T> where T : IBundleTevent; interface IBundlePriceTevent<out T> : IBundleTevent, IPublisherTevent<T> where T : IPriceTevent; interface IBundleReviewsTevent<out T> : IBundleTevent, IPublisherTevent<T> where T : IReviewTevent; abstract class BundleTevent : TaggregateTevent, IBundleTevent { protected BundleTevent() {} BundleTevent(TaggregateId taggregateId) : base(taggregateId) {} internal class Created(TaggregateId taggregateId, string name) : BundleTevent(taggregateId), IBundleTevent.ICreated { public string Name { get; } = name; } } class BundleTevent<T>(T tevent) : TaggregateTevent<T>(tevent), IBundleTevent<T> where T : IBundleTevent; class BundlePriceTevent<T>(T tevent) : BundleTevent, IBundlePriceTevent<T> where T : IPriceTevent { public T Tevent { get; } = tevent; } class BundleReviewsTevent<T>(T tevent) : BundleTevent, IBundleReviewsTevent<T> where T : IReviewTevent { public T Tevent { get; } = tevent; } class Bundle : Taggregate<Bundle, IBundleTevent, BundleTevent, IBundleTevent<IBundleTevent>, BundleTevent<BundleTevent>> { static class Slots { internal static readonly SharedTomponentSlot<Bundle, IBundleTevent, BundleTevent, IPriceTevent, IBundlePriceTevent<IPriceTevent>> Price = new(typeof(BundlePriceTevent<>), static bundle => bundle.Price); internal static readonly SharedTomponentSlot<Bundle, IBundleTevent, BundleTevent, IReviewTevent, IBundleReviewsTevent<IReviewTevent>> Reviews = new(typeof(BundleReviewsTevent<>), static bundle => bundle.Reviews); } static readonly TeventRouting<Bundle, IBundleTevent> Appliers = DeclareAppliers(it => it .For<IBundleTevent.ICreated>(static (bundle, created) => bundle.Name = created.Name) .SharedTomponent(Slots.Price) .SharedTomponent(Slots.Reviews)); protected override TeventRouting TeventAppliers => Appliers; Bundle() { Price = new Price(Slots.Price.In(this)); Reviews = new SharedTentityCollection<Review, ReviewId, IReviewTevent, IReviewTevent.IWritten>(Slots.Reviews.In(this)); } public string Name { get; private set; } = ""; public Price Price { get; } public SharedTentityCollection<Review, ReviewId, IReviewTevent, IReviewTevent.IWritten> Reviews { get; } public static Bundle Create(string name) { var bundle = new Bundle(); bundle.Publish(new BundleTevent.Created(new TaggregateId(), name)); return bundle; } public Review AddReview(int stars) => Reviews.AddByPublishing(new ReviewTevent.Written(ReviewId.New(), stars)); } The price and the review are written once, each: Its tevent interfaces, rooted in an interface of its own that implements ITevent, or ISharedTentityTevent<TId> for a shared tentity, and the classes implementing them. Its class, deriving from SharedTomponent<> or SharedTentity<,,,>, with its tevent routing. Each owner then writes, for each shared tomponent it holds: An adopting wrapper tevent: an interface that is a tevent of the owner and an IPublisherTevent<T> of the shared tomponent's tevents, and a class implementing it. A slot, in its nested Slots class, holding that class and how to get the shared tomponent from an owner. The slot, entered in its tevent routing: .SharedTomponent(Slots.Price). The shared tomponent, constructed with the slot in this owner: new Price(Slots.Price.In(this)).

Compze/Teventive/Taggregates/_docs/taggr.title: Taggregate Inheritance | Compze
Compze/Teventive/Taggregates/_docs/taggr.summary: Note Here we are entering less well charted waters. We are confident about the design we present here. However, full, support for routing tevents like this, and for building taggregates in this way, is still a work in progress. Taggregate Inheritance So far we have adressed the inheritance hierarchy of tevents within a single taggregate. Now let's look at what happens when we inherit one taggregate from another. Let's go with a trivial and classic example to make the point with as little distraction as possible. Animals. interface IAnimalTevent : ITaggregateTevent { interface IBorn : IAnimalTevent, ITaggregateCreatedTevent; } interface ICatTevent : IAnimalTevent; interface IDogTevent : IAnimalTevent; The problem Now imagine you're a dog person, you only care about when dogs are born. How would you listen to just the dog born tevents? Uh oh! You can't. There is only one IBorn and it is shared by all the animals. Much of the point of inheritance is to reuse functionality, so we can't very well require every inheriting class to reimplement birth using a different interface. That would defeat the point. Warning If you're thinking of using some sort of factory method pattern for generating the subclass tevents and adding inheriting interfaces for dogs. Don't. We tried it. And it turns out that you will have to mirror and duplicate the entire semantic hierarchy of the base class tevent interfaces for each inheriting class. It turns into an absolutely horrifying mess of duplication where the slightest misstep breaks things. We gave up entirely on inheriting taggregates when we had found no better way than that. Please, don't even try it. The solution Thankfully we eventually realized that there is an elegant simple solution built right into C#. This should be familiar: IEnumerable<object> objects = [new(), new()]; IEnumerable<string> strings = ["1", "2"]; objects = strings; Do you see it? Generic covariance! IEnumarable<string> is assignable to IEnumerable<object> and assignability is how we route tevents. Eureka! Well it turns out it works. (But requires a lot of major refactorings within Compze which are still ongoing.) Rather than try to twist english into a language capable of expressing what I'm talking about, which I'm finding unmanageable, I'll use C#. interface IAnimalTevent<out T> : ITaggregateTevent<T> where T : IAnimalTevent; interface ICatTevent<out T> : IAnimalTevent<T> where T : IAnimalTevent; interface IDogTevent<out T> : IAnimalTevent<T> where T : IAnimalTevent; So the wrapping interfaces, which take a type parameter, tell us only which class published the tevent. A Cat or a Dog instance (assuming Animal is abstract). The inner tevent is the real tevent that contains all the specifics of what happened. So actually, what a Dog publishes is never just IDogTevent, it is always IDogTevent<IAnimalTevent>, correspondingly a Cat publishes ICatTevent<IAnimalTevent> and the problem has been solved. Now you can listen to just the tevents from dogs by doing this: registrar .ForTevent<IDogTevent<IAnimalTevent.IBorn>>(born => { WriteLine($"Dog Id:{born.Tevent.TaggregateId} was born!"); return Task.CompletedTask; }); Do this if you only care about cats: registrar .ForTevent<ICatTevent<IAnimalTevent.IBorn>>(born => { WriteLine($"Cat Id:{born.Tevent.TaggregateId} was born!"); return Task.CompletedTask; }); This if you don't care what type of animal it was: registrar .ForTevent<IAnimalTevent.IBorn>(born => { WriteLine($"Animal Id:{born.TaggregateId} was born!"); return Task.CompletedTask; }); And this if you care about all animals, but need handle different animals differently: registrar .ForTevent<IAnimalTevent<IAnimalTevent.IBorn>>( born => { WriteLine($"{born.GetType().Name.Replace("Tevent", "")} Id: {born.Tevent.TaggregateId}, was born!"); return Task.CompletedTask; });

Compze/Teventive/Taggregates/_docs/teven.title: Tevent naming | Compze
Compze/Teventive/Taggregates/_docs/teven.summary: How to name tevents On the last page we were starting to run into some slightly unwieldy tevent names. Like IUserEmailPropertyUpdatedTevent. Now that it still reasonably readable and mostly unambiguous. That will not hold true as things get more complicated though if we keep naming tevents like that. Take this slightly more complicated tevent name for instance: IUserProfileNamePropertyUpdatedTevent. Is this a tevent published by a UserProfile taggregate? Or is it a tevent published by a Profile component within a User taggregate? Or is it a PropertyUpdatedTevent from the ProfileName component of the User taggregate? Imagine trying to untangle such questions when you have four or more levels of nested composition in your taggregate.... We've tried a number of different ways of dealing with tevent naming. One is using namespaces, which sounds like it should work. User.Tevents.ProfileComponent.PropertyUpdatedTevents.IName. Not too bad, right? Except when searching for types, or after your IDE helpfully simplifies references for you, you end up looking at just IName, which is unhelpful... registrar.ForTevent<IName>(nameTevent => { WriteLine("Uhmm... What is happening here?"); return Task.CompletedTask; }); The best structure we've found to deal with tevent naming is this: interface IUserTevent : ITaggregateTevent { internal interface IProfile : IUserTevent { internal interface IPropertyUpdated : IProfile { internal interface IName : IPropertyUpdated { string Name { get; } } } } } Nice and structured with each level of nesting inheriting from the previous level. Giving us: registrar .ForTevent<IUserTevent.IProfile.IPropertyUpdated.IName>(clarity => { WriteLine($"Ahh: {clarity.Name}"); return Task.CompletedTask; }); Readable and unambiguous. Not bad. Note We do not repeat Tevent for every level of nesting. And should you dislike the repeated I we do not condemn doing this: IUserTevent.Profile.PropertyUpdated.Name 😉

about/core-beliefs.html.title: Core beliefs | Compze
about/core-beliefs.html.summary: Core beliefs We believe that if you are considering using our tools you really should read all of this page to determine if it is likely to be a good fit for you and your organization. You may have trouble seeing the relevance at first, but it should all fit together as a whole in the end. We believe that people should always be a vital consideration:: We believe that our level of success of failure in collaborative endeavors hinges more on the humans, relationships and cultures involved than on any other factor. On how well we collaborate, communicate, motivate etc. We believe that this in turn hinges on our understanding of ourselves, on our understanding of human nature, on our understanding of the human mind and its properties, strengths and weaknesses. We believe that this understanding must include our drives, instincts, emotions and feelings. We believe that whenever we lose sight of this as a vital consideration when making choices we are likely to make choices with poor outcomes. This includes software design choices. We believe in the necessity of accepting complexity and letting go of certainty:: We believe we all instinctively prefer simplicity, certainty and absolutes. That this is a trait that was likely adaptive when we lived as hunter gatherers. We believe that this is no longer a primarily adaptive trait. We believe that succumbing to this trait cripples our ability to see the true complexity of the reality we have before us. Rather than clear cut wrong and right ways to do things we believe that we face great complexity and a great amount of possible choices in every situation. We believe that we must accept the weight of the uncertainty of this reality in order to make good choices. We believe in the superiority of motivated belief over dichotomies and absolutes:: We believe that succumbing to the desire to think and debate in terms of simple good versus bad dichotomies or absolutes such as "best way" is crippling. That it cripples not only our own understanding, but even more so our ability to collaborate in teams and larger communities. We believe that it is far better to say: "We believe" and then motivate that belief, than to state something as a fact without motivation. We believe that we must resist the temptation to talk about good versus bad and wrong versus right. We believe that there is no such thing as a "best" way to do anything, rather every option has a complex set of consequences in any specific set of circumstances which we never fully understand. We believe that we should abandon the false simplicity of right versus wrong dichotomies and absolutes such as "best". We believe that development should focus on shared mental models designed for humans:: We believe that developing software is first and foremost a process of collaboratively designing and communicating shared mental models. We believe that our focus must be on the quality and clarity of our mental models and the clarity and expressiveness of the code that we use to communicate these mental models to each other and our future selves. That the quality of a design is determined by how easily the totality of the mental models that it contains can be learned, communicated, and modified by human beings. We believe that the primary limiting factor is the mental burden imposed by the totality of our shared mental models:: We believe that in the majority of software development situations a lack of focus on the quality of the mental models is ultimately the primary factor limiting progress. That progress slows and ultimately stalls when the totality of our mental models fall into a state where the humans developing them can no longer effectively learn, understand, modify and communicate them. We believe that if we continually refactor our mental models to fit the human mind it is possible to maintain progress indefinitely without stalling and with limited slowdown even when facing immensely complicated software. We believe that this is the implicit principle underpinning approaches such as Domain Driven Design and principles such as SOLID.

about/faq_old.html.summary: How stable is Compze? The event store and the document database have been proven in production for a number of years. The current code has only minor changes. The service bus is new, under development, and untried in production. Of course all the components have test suites. No component has known bugs. We normally prioritize bug fixes over all feature development. What type of infrastructure does Compze require? Compze uses a relational database for all storage. Currently, supported databases are Sql Server, PostgreSql and MySql. Other than a Sql instance composable components have no special requirements. Performance & scalability How well does Compze components perform? Very well and it will only get better. We have spent a ton of effort making sure that both performance and scalability is as high as possible without sacrificing reliability, productivity and maintainability. We have automated performance degradation tests that run continuously as we develop. We continuously look for ways to make things even faster and as we do we adjust the tests to require the new level of performance that we have achieved. What if we need extreme querying scalability? Given this requirement we assume that you are willing to sacrifice some level of consistency in query results. These are then possible options: Maintain query models in any storage with sufficient scalablility. Add a layer on top of your querying API that makes use of a distributed cache. What if we need extreme write side scalability? If only a small subset of your data requires this level of write scalability, consider implementing only that part using other tools. If most of your data requires that level of scalability we would not recommend using our tools. Reliability Why do you enforce transactions for all updates? Because it is our opinion that without transactions you have to sacrifice either reliability or simplicity/maintainability and we prioritize those over scalability and performance. Why do you enforce exactly once delivery for domain events? Because it is our opinion that without exactly once delivery you have to sacrifice either reliability or simplicity/maintainability and we prioritize those over scalability and performance. I've heard that exactly once delivery is impossible... All arguments to that effect that we have encountered reason by disallowing transactions and/or message deduplication. Only through imposing this artificial constraint does exactly once delivery become "impossible". Exactly once == at least once + deduplication + transactions.

about/primary-architectural-choices.html.summary: Primary architectural choices We require you to learn a "new" modelling paradigm, semantic events:: We do not believe that we would be able to build highly complicated software using a language that did not support a flexible modelling paradigm, such as object oriented programming, without great loss of productivity, simplicity and safety. We believe that such standardized modelling paradigms enable us to successfully manage far greater levels of complexity than we could without them. This is what we aim to achieve by ubiquitously leveraging the semantic event modeling paradigm throughout our tools. Using the existing interface support in C# we enable you to model a highly complicated domain in terms of which events can occur and how the meanings of these events relate to each other, the aggregate root to which they belong, and to other abstractions in the domain. The same modelling paradigm is utilized at all levels of design. From the smallest component or entity nested in an aggregate to designing and implementing the highest level integrations in an ecosystem of integrated systems. Our experience is that this new modelling paradigm, this new view of your domain and ecosystem of domains, is highly beneficial to managing and scaling complexity of the domains and integrations between them. We also find it highly beneficial in communicating with with domain experts. It has given us an expressive way of viewing a system in terms of what can happen, without getting bogged down in the details of how. On the technical side it enables us to dramatically cut down on manual code and manual configuration. It enables us to build complicated aggregates, read models, and message based integrations with simple, SOLID, expressive code. All with zero manual routing code or configuration to take into consideration. You can use the same powerful mental model to understand how everything will work at all levels instead of having to design and remember countless custom routes within aggregates and within the bus. Our experience is that this as a whole dramatically reduces the total mental burden of understanding a large system or ecosystem of systems. Our experience is that it allows us to scale to far greater complexity of a domain and exposed features without development slowing or virtually stalling due to the runaway mental burden of an implementation that does not leverage a powerful modelling paradigm. We enforce the use of transactions for all domain data updates:: We enforce the use of exactly once delivery for domain events and commands::

index.html.summary: Ushering in paradigm shifts There are two areas where it seems to us like the industry has been stuck in old models for more than a decade. Failing to realize and leverage the potential of paradigms that are already here. Paradigms which can fundamentally transform how we build systems for the better. Compze aims to help make these paradigms widely understood, accessible, and popular through developing tooling and writing documentation: Teventive Leveraging .NET type compatibility, teventive programming enables an event modeling paradigm which Gives an unprecedented ability to understand domains in terms of how the events that can occur relate to each other. Eliminates all need for manual event routing and type checking. Dramatically reduces the number of event subscriptions needed. Enables modeling inheritance and composition of event based aggregates with elegant precision. Unifies fine-grained property-updated style events and coarse-grained domain events. Enables subscribing to precisely the event you need, while being guaranteed that when new events are added, inheriting the current event, you will receive those too without needing to change anything in your subscriber code. In spite of this, to this day, countless event driven applications are shock full of code that leverages none of these possibilities. Resulting in what can only be described as maintenance nightmares. It's essentially the event equivalent of working in C# while completely refusing to use generics and object-oriented programming. Surely we should not even need to argue that this is ill-advised? Typermedia APIs The most popular API in the world is a Browsable API (REST to be exact). You are using it right now. It's called the world wide web. Can you imagine trying to use it without links and forms? Imagine reading this page and instead of a link you are presented with: 4375. That is actually how we build most APIs today. Why? Typermedia expands on hypermedia thinking by leveraging the .NET type system to create APIs which: Can be fully explored using a navigator, browsed much like a website, by Getting links: tueries Posting forms: tommands All with full type safety and autocomplete in your IDE Can be in-process, or remote Routes tueries and tommands by their .NET types giving Zero configuration routing A simple already well known programming model. Further encapsulates your domain, exposing less implementation details than traditional services. Are excellently suited for building a Just-Beneath-The-UI-Rendering-Layer layer, ideal for black box testing. Once you've used APIs like that, how would you feel about an API that gives you an int instead of a link to the user?
